claims.text: The investigated equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy and its selected quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after standardized thermomechanical processing.
Local lattice distortion arising from compositional fluctuations is the primary determinant of mechanical-property differences among these FCC alloys.
Increasing the number of constituent elements enhances compositional heterogeneity.
Enhanced compositional heterogeneity increases local lattice distortion and associated strain fields.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation glide through solute-dislocation interactions.
Local lattice distortions can change the slip mode toward more curved, wavy, or heterogeneous dislocation paths.
Dislocation-solute interactions caused by lattice distortion increase yield strength.
Dislocation-solute interactions caused by lattice distortion modify ductility.
The equiatomic quinary alloy has greater local lattice distortion than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quaternary and ternary subsets have lower yield strength than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary subsets exhibit more planar slip than the equiatomic quinary alloy.
The greater lattice distortion in the quinary alloy may reduce its ductility relative to lower-component subsets.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to single-phase FCC alloys produced through similar thermomechanical routes.
The proposed relationship may not apply to non-equiatomic, multiphase, or substantially differently processed alloys.
Processing-induced residual stresses and other microstructural features can confound the relationship between compositional complexity, lattice distortion, and mechanical properties.
High-resolution XRD and TEM can quantitatively characterize the local lattice distortion or microstrain relevant to the proposed mechanism.
